concept_html:
Target leakage happens when a feature carries information that would not exist at the moment you make the prediction. The model learns the leak, scores brilliantly in validation, and fails in production, where the leak is absent.

Ask one question of every feature: would I know this value at prediction time?

Typical leaks in customer and survey data:

  • Consequences of the outcome. cancellation_reason predicts churn perfectly, because only churners have one. refund_amount predicts complaints.
  • Values measured after the prediction date. calls_to_support_last_30d computed on the extraction date, not the prediction date, includes calls made while the customer was leaving.
  • Proxies from the labelling process. A reviewed_by column that is only filled in for fraud cases.
  • IDs and timestamps that encode order. If churners were loaded in a later batch, a row ID predicts churn.

A quick screen catches the worst cases. Compute each feature's AUC on its own against the target. A single feature with an AUC near 1.0, or near 0.0 for an inverse relationship, deserves suspicion before celebration. With scikit-learn 1.8:

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
auc = roc_auc_score(y, X[col])
strength = max(auc, 1 - auc)

A screen does not prove leakage, and a leak spread across several features will pass it. The real defence is a feature timeline: for every feature, the date it becomes known, compared with the prediction date. Keep that table in the project and review it with someone who knows how the data is produced.

When in doubt, leave the feature out and measure how much the model loses. A feature worth 0.15 AUC on its own that nobody can explain is more likely a leak than a discovery.

lines: import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
LEAK_THRESHOLD = 0.95
def leakage_screen(X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series, threshold: float = LEAK_THRESHOLD) -> list[str]:
"""Numeric features that alone separate the classes suspiciously well."""
suspects = []
for col in X.select_dtypes("number").columns:
known = X[col].notna()
if known.sum() == 0 or y[known].nunique() < 2:
continue
auc = roc_auc_score(y[known], X.loc[known, col])
if max(auc, 1 - auc) >= threshold:
suspects.append(col)
return suspects

exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score


def leakage_screen(X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series, threshold: float = 0.95) -> list[str]:
    """Numeric features that alone separate the classes suspiciously well.

    Args:
        X: Candidate features.
        y: Binary target aligned with X.
        threshold: AUC strength at or above which a feature is flagged.

    Returns:
        Suspect column names, in column order.
    """
    suspects = []
    for col in X.select_dtypes("number").columns:
        known = X[col].notna()
        if known.sum() == 0 or y[known].nunique() < 2:
            continue
        auc = roc_auc_score(y[known], X.loc[known, col])
        if max(auc, 1 - auc) >= threshold:
            suspects.append(col)
    return suspects

title: Target leakage, features that know the answer
why_html: A churn model scored AUC 0.97 in validation. The top feature was days_since_last_login, computed on the day the training data was extracted. For churned customers, that included the weeks after they had already left. In production, scored on active customers, the model ranked customers little better than chance. The retention campaign built on it spent its budget on the wrong people for two months.
